## Your study preregistration journey

<br> <br> From: *“I am not sure what some of the opportunities are or
how to overcome some of the challenges of doing a preregistration* <br>
<br> To: "*“I feel able discuss the benefits and barriers of
preregistration and identify which part of a preregistration I can improve
on"*

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**:
In part 2 of this preregistration workshop I hope you will go from not being sure of the opportunities and challenges of doing a preregistration to being able to discuss benefits and barriers and identify an area of the preregistration process you can improve on.

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

## Quick recap from preregistration part I

-   Study preregistration is an open science practice that safe guard
    researchers from questionable research practices and biases by
    making decision-making processes more explicit.

-   It involves uploading a time-stamped, publicly-available record of a
    research study plan onto a register, which is given a unique and
    permanent study identifier
    
    
::: notes
**Presenter Notes**:

-   Study preregistration is an open science practice that safe guard

    permanent study identifier.

## Learning goals

**Aim**: Examine the benefits of preregistration to researchers and
wider research ecosystem, and discuss common challenges and how to
address them. <br> <br>

There are **two** sections to this submodule:

- **Section 1**: Benefits and barriers of preregistration

- **Section 2:** Building up skills in preregistration

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**:
The overall aim of this submodule is to examine the benefits of preregistration to researchers and wider research ecosystem, and discuss common challenges and how to
address them.

There are 2 sections: first we will discuss the benefits and barriers of doing a preregistration and then in the second section we will look at practicing improving our preregistration skills.


**Instructor Notes**:
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Section 1: Learning goals and overview

Section 1 is all about recognizing common benefits and barriers of
preregistration for researchers and wider research ecosystem <br> <br>

Activities: Quiz and self-reflection exercise

After completing section 1 you should be able to:

- **Explain** the perceived barriers to doing a preregistration
- **Identify** key benefits of preregistration

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**:
We will begin by outlining the common benefits and barriers of
preregistration for researchers and wider research ecosystem.

There will be a quiz at the end and along the way several self-reflection exercises.

After completing section 1 you should be able to:

- **Explain** the perceived barriers to doing a preregistration
- **Identify** key benefits of preregistration

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

Section 2 is about practicing improving a component of a study
preregistration <br> <br>

Activity: Build up your preregistration toolkit! (pair work)

After completing section 2 you should be able to:

- **Self-reflect** 
- **Propose** an action that follows the principles of study preregistration that one can implement

::: notes

In section 2 we turn our attention to building up our registration toolkit, by practicing improving a component of a study preregistration.


**Instructor Notes**:

## **Section 1**: Benefits and barriers of preregistration


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Benefits for researchers I

Improved planning and project management
- Outline data collection methods and analysis plans which reduces ambiguity and errors during data analysis stage

Builds your reputation
- Transparently show to the wider research community your plans and tests
- Signal that you have taken steps to mitigate against hindsight and confirmation bias (Wagenmakers & Dutilh, 2026)


::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Benefits for researchers II

Easier to write up and publish findings
- Front loading the thinking and planning makes writing up results and discussion a smoother process
- If preregistration is approved as a registered report during stage 1 journal peer review, you have "in-principle acceptance".

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Benefits for teams

Clearer involvement of collaborators/project partners
- Provides opportunities for project partners to discuss and refine plans before data collection
- Detailed research plans provide clarity for project partners, which is increasingly important in the era of large-scale collaborations

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Increase research credibility

## Barriers with preregistration


::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: 

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Challenges: time

Time: "I haven't got time to do a study registration"

- *Counterargument:* front-loaded effort during the planning stage can
  help later on during write up and during peer review.

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Challenges: incentives

Lack of incentives: "I don't see the point"

- *Counterargument:* aside from individual researcher benefits
  (increased reflection, reduced likelihood of systematic errors),
  journals are increasingly prioritizing study registrations.

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Challenges: overwhelm

Overwhelm: "There is so much that goes into a study registration"

- *Counterargument:* templates and FAQ pages can guide you and if you
  are unable to officially register a study, adopting principles of
  study registration is a good step (e.g. Open Science Buffet approach,
  @bergma2023)

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Challenges: lack of support

Lack of support: "No one in my team knows or cares about study
registration"

- *Counterargument:* share resources, and suggest a group meeting to
  discuss and learn more about study registration to increase
  familiarity.

::: callout-note
## Additional resource

Work through case study Paula’s Preregistration Problem
:::

::: notes
**Presenter Notes**: Script for the slide here.

**Instructor Notes**:
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary of section 1

- Lack of time or incentives are two common barriers to adopting the
  practice of study registration
- Important to discuss and address challenges
- Study registration does not prevent fraud or research misconduct (e.g.
  PARKing).


## Take home message

The principles and practice of study registration can feel like a steep
learning processes, adopting a few elements of study registration at a
time is good approach to working your way up completing a study
registration.



Reflection point Which benefit and barrier resonated with you most?
:::

## Improve the answer

- A research team wants to do a study on the topic of how indoor plants
  impact a person’s mood.
- Take a look at this research question: how can it be improved?

*How do indoor plants benefit people?*

1.  *think* about answer on your own
2.  *discuss* answer with neighbor and *write* out a joint answer
3.  we will *share* our answers in class


## Guiding questions

- How would you measure “benefit”?
- How would you study the interaction between plants and people?


::: notes
*Presenter Notes:*
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Exercise 3: answer

*From:* How do indoor plants benefit people?

<br>

*To:* How does having physical contact with indoor plants reduce
psychological and physiological stress in young-adult office workers?


Notice how the improved answer states the type of interaction between
plants and people, more specific details about types of benefits of
interest and the target demographic (e.g. young-adult office workers).

## Code blocks

```{r}
# A basic R code chunk
x <- 1:10
mean(x)

# A simple plot
hist(rnorm(100), main = "Histogram of Random Normals")

```

::: notes
**Note**: PowerPoint *cannot run R code*, therefore the code block this
will appear as *formatted code text*, not executed output.

## Interactive slide with questions + answers - not possible in pptx

Decide whether each scenario is an example of **reproducibility** or
**replicability**.

1.  A computational neuroscientist reruns a published fMRI analysis
    using the original dataset and Python scripts to verify the reported
    brain activation patterns.\
    **Answer:** Reproducibility

2.  An environmental scientist repeats a field experiment on soil
    nutrient levels using the same sampling protocol at a different
    site.\
    **Answer:** Replicability

3.  A linguist reanalyzes a corpus of historical texts using the same
    annotation guidelines and code to verify reported patterns of
    syntactic structures.\
    **Answer:** Reproducibility

## Features supported in html but not pptx

Here is an overview of which features cannot be transferred to a pptx
file from Quarto reveal js file:

- Custom HTML/CSS layout
  - Absolute positioning (position: absolute)
  - Flexbox / Grid layout
  - Custom margins, padding, alignment

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Features supported in html but not pptx

(continued)

- Fragments / incremental reveal
  - Click-to-reveal bullets or elements (.fragment)
  - Animations & transitions
  - CSS animations (@keyframes)
  - Reveal.js slide transitions (fade, zoom, etc.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Features supported in html but not pptx

(continued)

- Interactive JavaScript components
  - Plotly, Shiny apps, interactive charts
  - Custom JS widgets
  - Embedded iframes and external content
  - YouTube embeds
  - Google Maps
  - Embedded websites

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Features supported in html but not pptx

(continued)

- Dynamic sizing / responsive behavior

  - Percent-based sizing (width: 50%)

- Text shadows, letter spacing

- Custom tables with HTML styling

- Colored headers or rows

- Cell borders and padding via CSS

- Overlapping or rotated elements

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Features supported in html but not pptx

(continued)

- Rotated images or text

- Speech bubbles and callout shapes

- Bubble-style layouts

- Decorative shapes using CSS

- Embedded fonts and icon libraries

- Interactive quizzes or logic
